Patient Vignette: "Elena"

Elena is a 37-year-old musician who has been in a committed relationship with her partner, Marcus, for six years. She presents as thoughtful and articulate, with a careful, measured way of speaking that sometimes pauses mid-sentence, as if she is listening for something just out of earshot.

The trauma happened three years ago, on a warm summer evening. Elena was playing an outdoor jazz festival in a downtown plaza. She was on stage, mid-set, her fingers moving across the keys of her upright piano, when the first explosion ripped through the crowd. She remembers the sound not as a boom but as a physical pressure—a sudden, violent compression of the air that knocked the wind out of her and sent the piano lurching sideways. For a moment, she thought it was part of the sound system, a catastrophic feedback loop. Then the screaming started.

She doesn't remember how she got off the stage. She remembers the metallic smell of blood and dust, the sight of a saxophone lying in a puddle of red, the wet, ragged sound of a man gasping for air beside a toppled food cart. She remembers running, her legs moving without her permission, her hands still curled as if holding a chord. She found a doorway and pressed herself into it, her heart hammering so hard she thought it would crack her ribs. She stayed there for what felt like hours, though it was probably twenty minutes, listening to the sirens and the shouts and the terrible silence that followed.

In the weeks afterward, Elena tried to return to normal. She went back to her apartment, to Marcus, to her piano. But the piano felt wrong. The keys were too cold, too hard. When she played, she couldn't hear the music—only the memory of that sound, the one that had torn the world apart. She stopped performing. She stopped composing. She told herself she just needed a break, that the creative well was dry.

Now, three years later, Elena works as a session musician for a recording studio, but only from home. She records isolated piano tracks on a digital keyboard, sending them via email. She never meets the artists. She never goes to the studio. The thought of a room full of people, of a stage, of a crowd, makes her stomach clench. She avoids public transit, large gatherings, and any street that has a plaza or an outdoor cafe. She takes long, circuitous routes to the grocery store, always scanning for exits, always watching the faces of strangers for a flicker of intention.

Her sleep is fragmented. She wakes at 3:17 AM almost every night—the time she first looked at her watch while crouched in that doorway. She has nightmares that are not replays of the bombing but are instead filled with dissonant, wrong-sounding music: a piano that plays only the note F-sharp, over and over; a melody that spirals downward into a low, grinding hum. Marcus has learned not to touch her when she cries out in her sleep. She has snapped at him too many times, mistaking his hand on her shoulder for a stranger's grip.

She is irritable, easily startled. A car backfiring on her street sends her to the floor, heart racing. A sudden knock at the door makes her freeze, her breath shallow, until she can confirm who it is through the peephole. She has stopped going to concerts, even small ones. She has stopped listening to jazz entirely. The genre that was her life now feels like a trigger, a language she no longer speaks.

Elena describes her current state as "living in a muted world." She says she feels like she is wrapped in a thick blanket, unable to feel joy or excitement, only a constant, low-grade vigilance. She loves Marcus, but she knows she has pulled away from him, that she is brittle and quick to anger. She wants to play again—really play, in front of people, with the full weight of her body behind the keys. But every time she sits down to try, her hands hover over the keyboard, and she hears that first, terrible compression of air.
